chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
title: The September 1945 pick-up session with 'Wingy' Mesheux
summary: Moore identifies the trumpeter as a New York dentist with an artificial hand called Wingy.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Right, that's a trio. I think I sent you some of that on the tape. That was in April. Then in September of that year, you recorded with Oliver Mesheux, the trumpet player, and Omer Simeon on clarinet, and Pops Foster on bass, with Art Hodes.
Yeah.

That was a quintet. You played "Jack Daley Blues," "Blues For Jelly," "Beale Street Blues" -- which was never put out. But was this just a pick-up group for recording? Or were these musicians part of the Art Hodes group at the time?
That was a pick-up group for recording.
I see. Who was Oliver Mesheux?
Did he play trumpet?
He was the trumpet player on those recordings.
Moore (III) - 39
Yeah. He was a ...(?)... But he was a very good trumpet player. He was a dentist by trade.
Oh, is that right?
Yeah. A dentist.
He lived here in New York.
Yes.
And he practiced here in New York.
Yes. We called him Wingy for short, because he had one arm...one hand, rather...
One hand?
Yeah, he had an artificial hand.
And he was a dentist also.
Yeah, he was a dentist.
Hmm, interesting.
But he loved to play his horn. He played pretty good. He played nice.
